planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; native to cold mountain meadows of Siberia and the Tian Shan, this is one of the hardiest and easiest fritillaries to grow, tolerating heavier soil and more moisture than desert-dwelling relatives.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade or full sun for April-May bloom; pale yellow fritillary sends up sturdy stems clothed in glaucous, blue-green foliage and topped by two to six nodding, broadly bell-shaped flowers in soft, muted greenish-yellow, faintly washed with dusky purple tessellation on the inner surface. Native to high mountain meadows and scrub of Siberia, Kazakhstan, and the Tian Shan range of western China, it is exceptionally cold-hardy and, unlike many showier fritillaries, tolerates ordinary garden soil and a degree of summer moisture without rotting. It naturalizes slowly by offsets in a woodland-edge or rock garden setting and combines well with other early-spring bulbs under deciduous shrubs. Allow foliage to yellow and die back fully before removing it.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; chocolate lily is a Pacific coast woodland and grassy-bluff native ranging from British Columbia to California and grows best with the light, dappled shade and leaf-litter soil of an open oak or conifer woodland.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade for a March-May bloom; chocolate lily bears one to several nodding, bell-shaped flowers in a distinctive checkered pattern of deep maroon-brown mottled with dull yellow-green, giving rise to both of its common names. It occurs naturally in open woodland, grassy bluffs, and coastal prairie from British Columbia south through California, typically in soil that is moist in winter and spring but dries somewhat by summer. The bulb is surrounded by numerous small rice-grain bulblets, historically gathered and eaten by Coast Salish and other Pacific Northwest peoples. In the garden, plant it beneath deciduous shrubs or among other woodland natives such as trillium and fawn lily, and leave clumps undisturbed to slowly increase by offsets.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in a warm, sheltered, sharply drained site in full sun in fall, 6-10 weeks before first frost; a smaller-scale relative of the crown imperial, it blooms earlier than F. imperialis and needs the same perfect drainage and dry summer dormancy.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun in fall for very early spring bloom, often the first fritillary to flower. Radde's fritillary is a smaller, more modest relative of the crown imperial, sending up a stout stem topped by a whorl of several pendant, creamy yellow-green bells beneath a tuft of leafy bracts — the same general architecture as F. imperialis but on a more compact plant with softer, less strongly scented flowers. Native to rocky slopes and scrub in Iran, Turkmenistan, and Afghanistan, it demands sharp drainage and a baked, dry dormancy through summer, performing best in a raised bed, gravel garden, or sheltered border against a warm wall. Once established it slowly increases by offsets and is a welcome, unusual accent among the earliest bulbs of the year.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; one of the more adaptable and easily grown fritillaries, at home at a woodland edge or in a sunny border.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade or full sun for April bloom. Pontic fritillary carries one or two large, solitary, bell-shaped flowers in soft sage-green, flushed and streaked with dull purple-brown at the base of each tepal, held above glaucous, blue-green foliage on sturdy stems. Native to woodland margins, scrub, and mountain meadows across the Balkans and northwestern Turkey along the Black Sea coast, it is considerably more forgiving of ordinary garden conditions than many alpine fritillaries and naturalizes readily at a woodland edge or in a lightly shaded border. Leave the foliage to yellow and wither naturally after bloom, and divide congested clumps of offsets after several years if flowering declines.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun to light shade; native to rocky Aegean and Turkish hillsides, it needs a dry summer dormancy and resents heavy, wet soils.

directions: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun to light shade in fall for early to mid-spring bloom. Elwes' fritillary sends up a single wiry stem bearing one or occasionally two narrow, nodding, bell-shaped flowers in dusky grey-green, faintly checkered with dull purple-brown, giving the blooms a quiet, understated elegance suited to a rock garden or alpine trough. Native to rocky hillsides and olive groves of the Aegean islands and western Turkey, it requires the sharp drainage and baked, dry summer rest of its native limestone habitat, making it a good candidate for a raised bed or scree planting rather than an ordinary border. Once settled into conditions it likes, it slowly multiplies by bulb offsets to form a modest colony.

planting.note: Plant the large bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in fertile, humus-rich soil that is moist through the growing season; Zwanenburg is a named Dutch selection prized for its richer, more saturated violet-blue flower color than the wild species.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in fall in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade for a late-spring display. Zwanenburg is a selected form of Cusick's camas chosen for its deeper, more intensely saturated steel-blue to violet-blue flower color compared with the paler blue of the straight species, carried in the same dense, many-flowered racemes on stout stems well above strappy foliage. It shares the species' unusually large bulbs, which make it one of the more reliable camassias to establish from purchased stock, and it naturalizes over time in a moist meadow or woodland-edge planting. Let the foliage die back completely and naturally after flowering before removing it, since the bulb is recharging for the following spring.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Blue Melody is grown as much for its creamy white-edged, variegated foliage as for its violet-blue flowers.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade for a late-spring display. Blue Melody is an unusual variegated sport of common camas, its strappy leaves edged in a crisp band of creamy white that brightens the planting from the moment growth emerges in early spring, well before the star-shaped, violet-blue flower spikes appear. The foliage effect remains attractive even after bloom fades, making it a more multi-season option than the plain species for the front of a moist border or naturalized meadow planting. Give it the same seasonally moist spring, drier summer dormancy that common camas prefers, and allow foliage to die back fully before cutting it back.
sources: Great Plant Picks — Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden

planting.note: Plant tubers 2-3 inches deep as soon as available in late summer or early fall, in moist, humus-rich, alkaline-leaning soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees; soak dry tubers 24 hours before planting to rehydrate them.

directions: Plant tubers 2-3 inches deep as early in fall as they can be obtained, in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees for late-winter bloom. Cilician winter aconite closely resembles the more familiar Eranthis hyemalis but bears noticeably larger, brighter golden-yellow flowers atop finely dissected, bronze-tinted young foliage that matures to green as the ruff-like collar expands beneath each bloom. Native to rocky woodland and scrub from Turkey through the Caucasus and Levant, it tends to flower a little later than E. hyemalis and tolerates slightly warmer winters, making it a useful choice for gardens at the milder edge of winter aconite's range. Like its relative, it resents disturbance once established and is best left undisturbed to self-seed and slowly form colonies beneath deciduous shrubs and trees.
